rows.stem: A man whose father was colour-blind marries a woman who had a colour-blind mother and normal father. What percentage of male children of this couple will be colour-blind ?
rows.solution:
A son receives his X chromosome from his mother and his Y chromosome from his father, so the man's own father being colour-blind has no bearing on the sons of this couple.

The woman's mother was colour-blind (\(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\text{X}^{\text{c}}\)), so she must have passed an \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\) to her daughter, while the normal father passed a normal X. The woman is therefore a **carrier**, \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\text{X}\).
- Half her eggs carry \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\) and half carry X.
- Every son gets one of these together with the father's Y, so half the sons are \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\text{Y}\) (colour-blind) and half are XY (normal).

So 50% of the male children will be colour-blind. So the answer is option (C) 50%.

rows.stem: GEAC stands for
rows.solution: GEAC is the **Genetic Engineering Approval Committee**, set up by the Indian Government to decide on the validity of GM research and on the safety of introducing genetically modified organisms for public services. So the answer is option (D) Genetic Engineering Approval Committee.

rows.stem:
Match the items in Column-A with that of Column-B :
| Column-A | Column-B |
|---|---|
| (i) Lady bird beetle | (a) Methanobacterium |
| (ii) Mycorrhiza | (b) Trichoderma |
| (iii) Biological control | (c) Aphids |
| (iv) Biogas | (d) Glomus |
Choose the option that matches the items of Column A with that of B correctly :
rows.solution:
- (i) Lady bird beetle: a biocontrol agent that feeds on **aphids**, so (i)-(c).
- (ii) Mycorrhiza: the symbiotic association of fungi of the genus **Glomus** with plant roots, so (ii)-(d).
- (iii) Biological control: **Trichoderma**, free-living fungi in the root ecosystem, are effective biocontrol agents of several plant pathogens, so (iii)-(b).
- (iv) Biogas: **Methanobacterium** and other methanogens produce large amounts of methane in the biogas plant, so (iv)-(a).

So the correct matching is (i)-(c), (ii)-(d), (iii)-(b), (iv)-(a), which is option (B).

rows.stem: The process of mineralization by microorganisms help in the release of :

options.label: B
options.text: both organic and inorganic nutrients from detritus.

options.label: D
options.text: inorganic nutrients from detritus and formation of humus.

rows.solution: Decomposition of detritus by microbes forms **humus** (humification), a dark amorphous substance that is highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes very slowly. In **mineralization**, the humus is further degraded by some microbes and **inorganic nutrients are released** into the soil. So the answer is option (A) inorganic nutrients from humus.

rows.stem: Transplantation of tissues/organs to some patients often fails due to rejection of such tissues/organs by the body of the patient. Which type of immune response is responsible for such rejections ?
rows.solution: The body can distinguish 'self' from 'non-self', and the rejection of a transplanted tissue or organ that is not well matched is due to the **cell-mediated immune response**, carried out by T-lymphocytes. This is why tissue matching and blood group matching are essential before a transplant, and why the patient has to take immunosuppressants afterwards. So the answer is option (D) Cell mediated immune response.

rows.stem:
Match the following items of Column-I with that of Column-II :
| Column-I | Column-II |
|---|---|
| (a) Trophoblast | (i) Embedding of blastocyst in the endometrium |
| (b) Implantation | (ii) Group of cells that would differentiate as embryo |
| (c) Inner cell mass | (iii) Embryo with 8-16 blastomeres |
| (d) Morula | (iv) Outer layer of blastocyst |
Choose the option that matches Column-I with Column-II correctly.
rows.solution:
- (a) Trophoblast: the **outer layer** of the blastocyst, which gets attached to the endometrium, so (a)-(iv).
- (b) Implantation: the **embedding of the blastocyst in the endometrium** of the uterus, so (b)-(i).
- (c) Inner cell mass: the group of cells attached to the trophoblast that **differentiate as the embryo**, so (c)-(ii).
- (d) Morula: the **embryo with 8–16 blastomeres**, so (d)-(iii).

So the answer is option (A) (a)-(iv), (b)-(i), (c)-(ii), (d)-(iii).

rows.stem:
The diagram given below shows labelling of four parts of a dicot embryo during its development as P, Q, R and S.
Choose the option that indicates correct labelling of 'P', 'Q', 'R' and 'S' of embryo in different stages of its development :

options.label: A
options.text: P: Egg, Q: Suspensor, R: Radicle, S: Cotyledon

options.label: B
options.text: P: Zygote, Q: Suspensor, R: Cotyledon, S: Plumule

options.label: C
options.text: P: Egg, Q: Radicle, R: Suspensor, S: Cotyledon

options.label: D
options.text: P: Zygote, Q: Suspensor, R: Cotyledon, S: Radicle

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a boxed row of five drawings joined by arrows, from a single cell through a two-celled stage, a globular embryo and a heart-shaped embryo to a mature embryo, captioned 'Globular embryo', 'Heart-shaped embryo' and 'Mature embryo', with leader lines P, Q, R and S; which structure each letter points to IS the answer, so it is withheld here. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The figure traces the development of a dicot embryo.
- P, the single cell at the start, is the **zygote**; the embryo develops from the zygote, not from the unfertilised egg.
- Q, the row of cells joining the embryo to its attachment, is the **suspensor**.
- R, the two lobes of the mature embryo, are the **cotyledons**.
- S, the stem tip lying between the cotyledons, is the **plumule**.

So the answer is option (B) P: Zygote, Q: Suspensor, R: Cotyledon, S: Plumule.

rows.subtopic: Isolation, Cutting and Amplification of DNA
rows.stem: Amplification of gene of interest by using DNA polymerase may go upto
rows.solution: In the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) the gene of interest is copied repeatedly, using two sets of primers and a thermostable DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase), through repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension. The DNA segment can be amplified to approximately **1 billion times**, that is, 1 billion copies are made. So the answer is option (C) 1 billion times.

rows.stem: The sequence of nitrogenous bases in a segment of a coding strand of DNA is 5' – AATGCTAGGCAC – 3'. Choose the option that shows the correct sequence of nitrogenous bases in the mRNA transcribed by the DNA.
rows.solution:
The mRNA is transcribed on the template strand, so its sequence is the same as that of the **coding strand**, with the same 5' to 3' polarity, except that uracil (U) replaces thymine (T).
- Coding strand: 5' – AATGCTAGGCAC – 3'
- mRNA: 5' – AAUGCUAGGCAC – 3'

So the answer is option (B) 5' – AAUGCUAGGCAC – 3'.

rows.stem: How many pollen grains and ovules are likely to be formed in the anther and the ovary of an angiosperm bearing 50 microspore mother cells and 50 megaspore mother cells respectively ?
rows.solution:
- **Pollen grains**: each microspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to form a tetrad of four microspores, each of which develops into a pollen grain. So 50 microspore mother cells give \(50 \times 4 = 200\) pollen grains.
- **Ovules**: an ovule has a single megaspore mother cell, which forms four megaspores by meiosis; three of these degenerate and only one becomes functional and develops into the embryo sac. So 50 megaspore mother cells correspond to 50 ovules.

So the answer is option (B) 200, 50.

rows.stem: Evolution of modern man involves the following man-like primates. Choose the correct series of human evolution.

options.label: A
options.text: Dryopithecus \(\rightarrow\) Homo erectus \(\rightarrow\) Australopithecines \(\rightarrow\) Homo sapiens

options.label: B
options.text: Australopithecines \(\rightarrow\) Homo erectus \(\rightarrow\) Neanderthal \(\rightarrow\) Homo sapiens

options.label: D
options.text: Homo erectus \(\rightarrow\) Australopithecines \(\rightarrow\) Homo sapiens \(\rightarrow\) Neanderthal

rows.stem:
RNA interference (RNAi) helps in making tobacco-plant resistant to a nematode (Meloidegyne incognitia)
Choose the correct option that shows how RNAi is achieved :

options.label: A
options.text: Preventing the process of translation of mRNA of the nematode.

options.label: B
options.text: Preventing the process of replication of DNA of the nematode.

options.label: C
options.text: Preventing the process of transcription of DNA of the plant.

options.label: D
options.text: Preventing the process of replication of DNA of the plant.

rows.solution: RNA interference silences a specific mRNA. Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes are introduced into the tobacco plant so that they produce both sense and antisense RNA. The two RNAs are complementary, so they form double-stranded RNA, which binds to the specific mRNA of the nematode and prevents its **translation**. The parasite cannot survive in a transgenic host expressing this interfering RNA, so the plant is protected. So the answer is option (A) Preventing the process of translation of mRNA of the nematode.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Saheli is the World's first non-steroidal oral contraceptive pill.
Reason (R) : It has been developed by National Institute of Immunology, New Delhi.
rows.context: For Question numbers 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Answer these questions by selecting the appropriate option given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: Saheli, the once-a-week pill, is a **non-steroidal** oral contraceptive, and it was the world's first such pill. The Reason is false: Saheli was developed by scientists at the **Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow**, not by the National Institute of Immunology, New Delhi. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : One of the property of genetic code is degeneracy.
Reason (R) : Some amino acids can be coded by more than one codon.
rows.context: For Question numbers 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Answer these questions by selecting the appropriate option given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: degeneracy is a property of the genetic code. The Reason is also true and is exactly what degeneracy means: some amino acids are coded by more than one codon (there are 61 coding codons for 20 amino acids). So both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : A bioreactor provides the optimal conditions for achieving the desired product by providing optimum growth conditions.
Reason (R) : The most commonly used bioreactors are of stirring type.
rows.context: For Question numbers 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Answer these questions by selecting the appropriate option given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: a bioreactor provides the optimal conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen) needed to achieve the desired product, which is why large volumes of culture are processed in it. The Reason is also true: the most commonly used bioreactors are of the stirring type. But the type of stirring does not explain why a bioreactor provides optimal conditions; it is only one design used to mix the contents and keep oxygen available. So both statements are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion, which is option (B).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : When the two genes in a dihybrid cross are situated on the same chromosome, the proportion of parental gene combinations is much higher than non-parental type.
Reason (R) : Higher parental gene combinations can be attributed to crossing over between two genes.
rows.context: For Question numbers 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Answer these questions by selecting the appropriate option given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: when two genes in a dihybrid cross lie on the same chromosome, the proportion of parental gene combinations is much higher than the non-parental type. The Reason is false: the high frequency of parental combinations is due to **linkage**, the physical association of the genes on one chromosome. Crossing over (recombination) between the genes produces the non-parental combinations, so it lowers, not raises, the share of parental types. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.stem: How are morphine and heroin related ? Mention their effect on the human body.
rows.solution:
- **Relation**: morphine and heroin are both **opioids**. Morphine is extracted from the latex of the poppy plant, Papaver somniferum, and heroin (commonly called smack) is chemically **diacetylmorphine**, obtained by the acetylation of morphine.
- **Effects on the body**:
  - morphine is a very effective **sedative and painkiller**, and is very useful in patients who have undergone surgery;
  - heroin is a **depressant** and slows down body functions.

rows.stem:
(i) Name an alcoholic drink which is produced by the help of microbes :
(1) With distillation
(2) Without distillation
(ii) Explain how cyanobacteria can be used as bio-fertilizer.
rows.solution:
(i) Brewer's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, is used to ferment malted cereals and fruit juices to produce ethanol.
- (1) With distillation: **whisky, brandy or rum**.
- (2) Without distillation: **wine or beer**.

(ii) Cyanobacteria are autotrophic microbes widely distributed in aquatic and terrestrial environments, and many of them (for example Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria) can **fix atmospheric nitrogen**. In paddy fields they serve as an important biofertiliser. Blue-green algae also **add organic matter to the soil and increase its fertility**.

rows.stem:
Analyse the following ecosystems and discuss, which will be more productive in terms of primary productivity :
A young forest, a natural old forest, a shallow polluted lake.
rows.solution:
The **natural old forest** will be the most productive of the three in terms of primary productivity.
- A natural old forest has a large number of trees and plants of many kinds, arranged in layers, so its dense canopy traps and uses most of the incident solar radiation in photosynthesis.
- A young forest is still developing; it has fewer trees and an incomplete canopy, so it captures less of the solar radiation than the old forest.
- A shallow polluted lake has fewer producers and a large amount of dead organic matter, so its primary productivity is lower than that of the natural old forest.

Note that productivity is a rate of production of organic matter, not the amount of biomass present (the standing crop). An old forest has a high gross primary productivity, but much of it is used up in respiration; a young, actively growing forest can show a higher net primary productivity, and the answer depends on which of the two is meant.

rows.stem: Differentiate between Net primary productivity and Gross primary productivity in an ecosystem.
rows.solution:
| Net primary productivity | Gross primary productivity |
|---|---|
| Gross primary productivity minus the respiration losses (R) of the producers: NPP = GPP \(-\) R. | The rate of production of organic matter by the producers during photosynthesis. |
| It is the biomass available for consumption by heterotrophs (herbivores and decomposers). | A considerable amount of it is used up by the plants themselves in respiration. |

rows.stem:
Study the cross given below :
Identify the abnormalities '1' and '2' in the offsprings of a cross done between a couple and distinguish between them.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a cross diagram: Parents 44 + XY and 44 + XX; Gametes 22 + XY and 22 + O from the first parent, 22 + X and 22 + X from the second; crossing lines lead to two bracketed Offsprings labelled '1' and '2'. Which gametes the lines join into each bracket decides the two abnormalities, so it is withheld here. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
- Offspring '1' is **Klinefelter's syndrome**, 44 + XXY: the 22 + XY sperm (from non-disjunction of the sex chromosomes in the father) fertilises a normal 22 + X egg.
- Offspring '2' is **Turner's syndrome**, 44 + XO: the 22 + O sperm, carrying no sex chromosome, fertilises a 22 + X egg.

| Klinefelter's syndrome | Turner's syndrome |
|---|---|
| An extra copy of the X chromosome: 47 chromosomes in all (trisomy of sex chromosomes). | Absence of one X chromosome: 45 chromosomes in all (monosomy of sex chromosomes). |
| A sterile male. | A sterile female. |
| Overall masculine development, with some feminine features such as gynaecomastia (development of breasts). | Rudimentary ovaries and a lack of other secondary sexual characters. |

rows.stem:
Study the pedigree chart given below, showing the inheritance pattern of blood group in a family :
Answer the following questions :
(a) Give the possible genotypes of individual 1 and 2.
(b) Which antigen or antigens will be present on the plasma membranes of the R.B.Cs of individuals '5' and '8' ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a pedigree whose symbols carry the blood groups, the only data the question has. Parents: 1 (square, B) and 2 (circle, A). Generation I, their children: 4 (square, A), 5 (square, AB), 6 (circle, B), 7 (square, A); 4 is married to 3 (circle, B). Generation II, children of 3 and 4: 8 (circle, O) and 9 (square, B). Stating the phenotypes does not state the genotypes asked for, so the chart is described in full. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(a) Individual 1 is blood group B and individual 2 is blood group A.
- Their child 6 is group B. Individual 2 (group A) cannot give \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\), so child 6 received \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) from 1 and **i** from 2.
- Their children 4 and 7 are group A. Individual 1 (group B) cannot give \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\), so they received \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\) from 2 and **i** from 1.

So individual 1 is \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\text{i}\) and individual 2 is \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\text{i}\). (This also fits individual 8: an O-group child, ii, of 3 and 4 needs an i from individual 4, who received it from individual 1.)

(b)
- Individual 5 is group AB, \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\text{I}^{\text{B}}\). The two alleles are co-dominant and both sugars are made, so **both antigen A and antigen B** are present on the plasma membrane of the RBCs.
- Individual 8 is group O, ii. Allele i produces no sugar, so **neither antigen A nor antigen B** is present.

rows.stem: A patient with ADA deficiency requires periodic infusion of genetically engineered lymphocytes. Explain why such periodic infusion is required and also suggest a permanent cure for such ADA deficiency.
rows.solution:
In gene therapy for ADA deficiency, lymphocytes from the patient's blood are grown in culture outside the body, a functional ADA cDNA is introduced into them using a retroviral vector, and the genetically engineered lymphocytes are returned to the patient.
- **Why periodic infusion**: these genetically engineered lymphocytes are **not immortal**, so as they die the patient needs a fresh infusion from time to time.
- **Permanent cure**: if the gene isolated from bone marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at **early embryonic stages**, it could be a permanent cure.

rows.stem: Describe in brief any two techniques that can be utilised to transfer recombinant DNA into the host cell directly without using any vector.
rows.solution:
Any two of these vector-less methods:
- **Micro-injection**: recombinant DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell.
- **Biolistics (gene gun)**: plant cells are bombarded with high-velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA.
- **Heat shock** (for bacterial cells): cells made competent with a divalent cation such as calcium are incubated with the recombinant DNA on ice, then placed briefly at \(42^\circ\text{C}\), and put back on ice, which forces the DNA into the cells.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the palindromic nucleotide sequence for following sequence of DNA segment :
5' – GAATTC – 3'
(b) Name the restriction endonuclease that recognizes this sequence.
(c) How are sticky ends produced ? Mention their role.
rows.solution:
(a) The given strand and its complementary strand are:
- 5' – GAATTC – 3'
- 3' – CTTAAG – 5'

The sequence is a **palindrome**: read in the same direction (5' to 3') on both strands, it reads GAATTC.

(b) This sequence is recognised by the restriction endonuclease **EcoRI**.

(c) Restriction enzymes cut the strand of DNA a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites, but **between the same two bases on the opposite strands**. EcoRI cuts between G and A on each strand. This leaves single-stranded portions, overhanging stretches (AATT) at the two ends, called **sticky ends**.

Role: sticky ends form **hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts**. Since the vector DNA and the foreign DNA are cut with the same enzyme, their sticky ends match, and this stickiness facilitates the action of the enzyme **DNA ligase** in joining them to form recombinant DNA.

rows.stem:
Study a part of life cycle of Plasmodium given below :
Answer the following questions :
(a) Name the infective stage of Plasmodium that is stored in the female Anopheles mosquito.
(b) Where does fertilization and development of parasite take place ?
(c) Identify labels P and Q in the given diagram.
(d) Asexual and sexual phase of the life cycle of the Plasmodium takes place in two different hosts. Write their names.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a drawing of part of the Plasmodium life cycle: a mosquito feeding on a human hand, a cluster of cells marked Q, a stage beside the caption 'Fertilization and development', and a rounded structure marked P at the top, joined by arrows; what P and Q are is asked in (c), so it is withheld here. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(a) **Sporozoites**, the infective stage, are stored in the salivary glands of the female Anopheles mosquito and are injected into a human with its bite.

(b) Fertilisation and development of the parasite take place in the **gut (stomach) of the female Anopheles mosquito**, after it takes up gametocytes with its blood meal.

(c)
- P: the **salivary gland of the female Anopheles mosquito**, where the sporozoites are stored.
- Q: **gametocytes**, the sexual stages that develop in the red blood cells of the human host and are taken up by the mosquito.

(d) The **asexual phase** takes place in the **human** host (in liver cells and red blood cells), and the **sexual phase** in the **female Anopheles mosquito**.

rows.stem:
(a) Indiscriminate human activities such as alien species invasion, fragmentation and habitat loss have accelerated the loss of biodiversity. Justify by taking one example for each.
(b) State the importance of the following :
(i) IUCN Red data list
(ii) Hot spots in conservation of biodiversity
rows.solution:
(a)
- **Alien species invasion**: the introduction of the Nile perch into Lake Victoria in East Africa led to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish in the lake. (Carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eichhornia) are other invasive species that threaten native species, as does the illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture, which threatens the indigenous catfishes.)
- **Habitat loss and fragmentation**: when large habitats are broken up into small fragments by human activities, mammals and birds that need large territories are badly affected, leading to population decline. The Amazon rain forest, harbouring probably millions of species, is being cut and cleared for cultivating soya beans or for conversion to grassland for raising beef cattle.

(b)
- (i) The **IUCN Red Data List** documents species under threat of extinction. It helps to identify and protect the species facing a high risk of extinction, and is crucial for conservation planning.
- (ii) **Biodiversity hot spots** are regions with very high levels of species richness and a high degree of endemism. Protecting them intensively, for example the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, could reduce the ongoing mass extinctions considerably.

rows.stem:
Study the diagram given below and answer the questions that follows :
(a) Identify the structure shown in the above figure.
(b) Identify the labels P and Q.
(c) Write the nature of histone proteins.
(d) Distinguish between Euchromatin and Heterochromatin.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a three-dimensional drawing of a strand wound around a ball-shaped core, with leader lines P (to the strand) and Q (to the core); naming the structure and its parts IS (a) and (b), so nothing more is said here. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
(a) The structure is a **nucleosome**, the unit of DNA packaging in eukaryotes.

(b)
- P: **DNA**, the negatively charged helix wrapped around the core.
- Q: **histone octamer**, the core of eight histone molecules.

(c) Histones are **basic proteins**: they are rich in the basic amino acid residues lysine and arginine, which carry positive charges in their side chains. This positive charge lets them hold the negatively charged DNA.

(d)
| Euchromatin | Heterochromatin |
|---|---|
| Loosely packed chromatin. | Densely packed chromatin. |
| Stains light. | Stains dark. |
| Transcriptionally active. | Transcriptionally inactive. |

rows.stem:
Shyam and Radha are expecting their first child with Radha being in her second month of pregnancy with no complications. Shyam's family has a history of cystic fibrosis while Radha's family has a history of Down's syndrome, leading to a concern that the baby may have one of these conditions.
(a) Suggest and explain a way of testing if their baby is at risk for any genetic disorders.
(b) In case of presence of one or both of the abnormalities and posing a risk to the mother's health, mention one possible option for them to consider. Is that option safe for Radha at the current gestational age ? Justify.
(c) Under what conditions is the process mentioned in (b) illegal ?
rows.solution:
(a) **Amniocentesis**: some of the amniotic fluid surrounding the developing foetus is taken out, and the foetal cells and dissolved substances in it are analysed to test for the presence of genetic disorders, such as Down's syndrome (a chromosomal disorder) or a single-gene disorder like cystic fibrosis.

(b) The option is **Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP)**, which is permitted where continuing the pregnancy poses a risk to the mother's health or where the foetus has a serious abnormality. **Yes**, it is safe for Radha: MTPs are considered relatively safe during the **first trimester, up to 12 weeks** of pregnancy, and she is in her second month.

(c) MTP is illegal and dangerous when it is **performed by unqualified quacks**, or when it is misused for **female foeticide**, that is, amniocentesis is used to find the sex of the foetus and a normal female foetus is then aborted.

rows.stem: Explain the basis on which gel electrophoresis technique works. Write any two ways the products obtained through this technique can be utilised.
Compare and contrast convergent and divergent evolution.
rows.solution:
**Differences**

| Divergent evolution | Convergent evolution |
|---|---|
| The same structure developed along different directions, owing to adaptations to different needs. | Different structures evolved for the same function and hence came to have similarities. |
| It produces **homologous** structures, for example the forelimbs of whales, bats, cheetahs and humans. | It produces **analogous** structures, for example the wings of a butterfly and of a bird. |
| It indicates **common ancestry**. | It indicates that similar habitats have resulted in the selection of similar adaptive features. |

**Similarities**
- Both are shaped by the environment, through natural selection acting on variation.
- Both contribute to the evolution of species.

rows.stem: Which hormone is responsible for the peak observed in Case 1 and Case 2 ? Write one function of that hormone.
rows.context: Study the graphs given below for Case 1 and Case 2 showing different levels of certain hormones and answer the question that follows :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:two boxed graphs, 'Case 1' and 'Case 2', each with a curve P rising to a point marked 'Peak', a dashed line marked 'Ovulation' with a small ovum sketch, a second curve Q, and the baseline marked 'Follicular Phase' and 'Luteal Phase'; Case 2 also has a curve marked 'HCG'. The hormones are not named and how Q and HCG run in each case is withheld, since it decides (a), (c) and (d). Page idx 16.
rows.solution: The peak is produced by the **luteinising hormone (LH)**. Both LH and FSH reach their peak in the middle of the cycle, and the rapid secretion of LH leading to its maximum level, the **LH surge**, induces the rupture of the Graafian follicle and so causes **ovulation**.

rows.stem: Write changes that take place in the ovary and uterus during follicular phase.
rows.context: Study the graphs given below for Case 1 and Case 2 showing different levels of certain hormones and answer the question that follows :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE:the case study's two hormone graphs (Case 1 and Case 2), attached so the context's 'graphs given below' is not left dangling; this sub-part is answerable from text. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
During the follicular (proliferative) phase:
- **Ovary**: under the stimulation of the gonadotropins (FSH and LH), the primary follicles in the ovary grow to become a fully mature **Graafian follicle**, which secretes estrogens.
- **Uterus**: the **endometrium of the uterus regenerates through proliferation**, under the influence of the estrogens.

rows.stem: Name the hormone Q of Case 2. Write one function of hormone Q.
rows.context: Study the graphs given below for Case 1 and Case 2 showing different levels of certain hormones and answer the question that follows :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the case study's two hormone graphs; Q is a curve named only by its letter and its shape in Case 2 is what identifies it, so the shape is withheld here. Page idx 16.
rows.solution: Hormone Q of Case 2 is **progesterone**, secreted by the corpus luteum. It is essential for the **maintenance of the endometrium**, which is needed for implantation of the fertilised ovum and for the other events of pregnancy.

rows.stem: Which structure in the ovary will remain functional in Case 2 ? How is it formed ?
rows.context: Study the graphs given below for Case 1 and Case 2 showing different levels of certain hormones and answer the question that follows :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the case study's two hormone graphs; what Case 2 represents is read from how its Q and HCG curves run, which is withheld here. Page idx 16.
rows.solution: The **corpus luteum** will remain functional in Case 2, which shows pregnancy (HCG is being secreted). It is formed after ovulation, when the **remaining parts of the Graafian follicle transform into the corpus luteum**. In pregnancy it does not degenerate, so it continues to secrete progesterone and maintain the endometrium.

rows.stem: The Monarch butterfly is highly distasteful to its predator because of a special chemical present in its body. How does the butterfly acquire this chemical ?
rows.context: In nature, we rarely find isolated, single individuals of any species; majority of them live in groups in a well-defined geographical area, share or compete for similar resources, potentially interbreed and thus constitute a population. The population has certain attributes whereas, an individual organism does not. A population at a given time is composed of individuals of different ages. The size of the population tells us a lot about its status in the habitat. Whatever ecological processes we wish to investigate in a population, be it the outcome of competition with another species, the impact of the predator or the effect of pesticide application, we always evaluate in terms of any change in the population size. The size, in nature, could be low or go into millions. Population size, technically called population density (N) need not necessarily be measured in numbers only. The size of a population for any species is not a static parameter. It keeps on changing with time depending on various factors including food availability, predation pressure and adverse weather.
rows.solution: The Monarch butterfly acquires this chemical during its **caterpillar stage, by feeding on a poisonous weed**. The chemical stays in its body, which makes the adult highly distasteful to its predators (birds).

rows.stem: If population density at a time t + 1 is 800, Emigration = 100, Immigration = 200, Natality = 200 and Mortality = 150, calculate the population density at time t and comment upon the type of age pyramid that will be formed in this case.
rows.context: In nature, we rarely find isolated, single individuals of any species; majority of them live in groups in a well-defined geographical area, share or compete for similar resources, potentially interbreed and thus constitute a population. The population has certain attributes whereas, an individual organism does not. A population at a given time is composed of individuals of different ages. The size of the population tells us a lot about its status in the habitat. Whatever ecological processes we wish to investigate in a population, be it the outcome of competition with another species, the impact of the predator or the effect of pesticide application, we always evaluate in terms of any change in the population size. The size, in nature, could be low or go into millions. Population size, technically called population density (N) need not necessarily be measured in numbers only. The size of a population for any species is not a static parameter. It keeps on changing with time depending on various factors including food availability, predation pressure and adverse weather.
rows.solution:
Population density changes as
\(N_{t+1} = N_t + [(B + I) - (D + E)]\),
where B is natality, I immigration, D mortality and E emigration.

\(800 = N_t + [(200 + 200) - (150 + 100)]\)

\(800 = N_t + (400 - 250) = N_t + 150\)

\(N_t = 800 - 150 = 650\)

So the population density at time t was **650**.

Comment: the population has grown from 650 to 800 in one time step, so it is an **expanding (growing) population**, and its age pyramid will be **triangular**, with a broad base of pre-reproductive individuals.

rows.stem:
Answer the following questions :
(i) State what do you understand by "MALT" ? Where it is located inside our body ?
(ii) Explain cytokine barriers.
(iii) Name the diagnostic test for AIDS. On what principle does it work ?
(iv) Bone marrow and thymus play an important role in human immune system. Explain how are they able to achieve this.
rows.solution:
(i) **MALT** is the **mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue**. It is located within the lining of the major tracts of the body: the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts. It constitutes about 50 per cent of the lymphoid tissue in the human body.

(ii) **Cytokine barriers**: virus-infected cells secrete proteins called **interferons**, which protect the non-infected cells from further viral infection. They are one of the barriers of innate immunity.

(iii) The widely used diagnostic test for AIDS is **ELISA (Enzyme Linked Immuno-Sorbent Assay)**. It works on the principle of **antigen–antibody interaction**. (PCR, which works by amplification of the viral nucleic acid, is also accepted.)

(iv) Bone marrow and thymus are the **primary lymphoid organs**, where immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes.
- The **bone marrow** is the main lymphoid organ, where all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are produced.
- The **thymus** is where some of these lymphocytes migrate and mature as T-lymphocytes.

Both the bone marrow and the thymus provide the micro-environment for the development and maturation of the T-lymphocytes, and this is how they play their role in the immune system.

rows.stem:
(i) Study the following table & fill 'H', 'I', 'J', 'K', 'L' and 'M' in following table with suitable words :
| | Chemical / Bioactive Molecule | Micro-organism | Category | Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | Butyric acid | H | I | Important applications in food, chemical & pharma industry |
| (b) | J | Monoscus purpureus | K | Inhibit cholesterol biosynthesis pathway |
| (c) | Cyclosporin A | L | Fungus | M |
(ii) Why are baculoviruses used as biological control agents ?
rows.solution:
(i)
- H: **Clostridium butylicum**, which produces butyric acid.
- I: **Bacterium**.
- J: **Statins**, which inhibit the enzyme of the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway and so act as blood-cholesterol lowering agents.
- K: **Yeast** (a fungus); the table's Monoscus purpureus is the yeast Monascus purpureus.
- L: **Trichoderma polysporum**, the fungus that produces cyclosporin A.
- M: an **immunosuppressive agent**, used in organ-transplant patients to suppress the immune system.

(ii) Baculoviruses (mostly of the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus) are used as biological control agents because:
- they are **species-specific, narrow-spectrum** insecticidal applications, so they attack only the target insects and arthropods;
- they have **no negative impact on non-target organisms**: plants, mammals, birds, fish or even other insects;
- so they are desirable in integrated pest management and in ecologically sensitive areas, where beneficial insects need to be conserved.

rows.stem:
(a) Distinguish between the two cells enclosed in a mature male gametophyte of an angiosperm.
(b) Study the diagram given below showing the modes of pollination. Answer the questions that follow.
(i) The given diagram shows three methods of pollen transfer in plants. Examine them carefully and write the technical terms used for pollen transfer methods '1', '2' and '3'.
(ii) How do the following plants achieve pollination successfully ?
(a) Water lily
(b) Vallisneria
(iii) Write advantages of pollen transfer in method '3'.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a boxed drawing of two flowering plants, the left one bearing two flowers on a forked stem and the right one a single flower, with three curved arrows numbered 1, 2 and 3 carrying pollen to a stigma; which flowers each arrow joins IS the answer to (b)(i), so it is withheld here. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(a)
| Vegetative cell | Generative cell |
|---|---|
| Bigger, with an abundant food reserve and a large, irregularly shaped nucleus. | Small and spindle-shaped, with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus; it floats in the cytoplasm of the vegetative cell. |
| Helps in the formation of the pollen tube. | Divides mitotically to form the two male gametes. |

(b)(i)
- Method '1' is **autogamy**: pollen is transferred from the anther to the stigma of the same flower.
- Method '2' is **geitonogamy**: pollen is transferred from the anther to the stigma of another flower on the same plant.
- Method '3' is **xenogamy**: pollen is transferred from the anther to the stigma of a flower on a different plant.

(ii)
- (a) **Water lily**: although aquatic, its flowers emerge above the level of the water and are pollinated by **insects or wind**, as in most land plants.
- (b) **Vallisneria**: pollinated by **water**. The female flower reaches the surface of the water on a long stalk, and the male flowers or pollen grains are released onto the surface; they are carried passively by water currents, and some of them reach the female flowers and their stigma.

(iii) Advantages of xenogamy (any two):
- it brings genetically different pollen grains to the stigma, so it produces **genetic variation** among the offspring;
- it avoids inbreeding depression and gives **healthier, more vigorous offspring** (heterosis);
- the variation helps adaptation and evolution, including the spread of traits such as disease resistance.

rows.stem:
Given below is the diagram of human ovum surrounded by a few sperms. Observe the diagram and answer the questions that follows :
(i) Compare the fate of sperms 'P', 'Q' and 'R' shown in the diagram.
(ii) Write the role of Zona pellucida in this process.
(iii) Analyse the changes occurring in the ovum after the entry of sperm.
(iv) How acrosome and middle piece of a human sperm are able to play an important role in human fertilization ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a human ovum with labels 'Ovum', 'Zona pellucida', 'Cells of the corona radiata' and 'Perivitelline space', approached by three sperms marked P, Q and R (one also labelled 'Sperm'); how far each sperm has got into the layers decides (i), so it is withheld here. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
(i) In the figure, sperm P has passed between the cells of the corona radiata and reached the zona pellucida, so **P is able to penetrate and fertilise the ovum**. Sperms Q and R are still outside, among or beyond the corona cells, and **Q and R are unable to enter or fertilise** the ovum, since the ovum allows only one sperm to fertilise it.

(ii) **Role of the zona pellucida**: when a sperm comes in contact with the zona pellucida layer of the ovum, it induces changes in the membrane that **block the entry of additional sperms**. This ensures that only one sperm fertilises the ovum.

(iii) The entry of the sperm **induces the completion of the meiotic division of the secondary oocyte**. This second meiotic division is unequal and forms a second polar body and a haploid ovum (the ootid). The haploid nucleus of the sperm and that of the ovum then fuse together to form a **diploid zygote**.

(iv)
- **Acrosome**: the cap-like structure on the anterior part of the sperm head is filled with **enzymes that help in fertilisation**, allowing the sperm to penetrate the layers around the ovum and enter its cytoplasm.
- **Middle piece**: it has **numerous mitochondria**, which produce the energy for the movement of the tail. This gives the sperm the motility essential for reaching the ovum and fertilising it.

rows.stem:
(i) Perform a cross between two sickle cell carriers. What ratio is obtained between carrier, disease free and diseased individuals in \(\text{F}_1\) progeny ? Name the nitrogenous base substituted, in the haemoglobin molecule in this disease.
(ii) Explain the difference in inheritance pattern of flower colour in garden pea plant and snap-dragon plant with the help of monohybrid crosses.
rows.solution:
(i) A sickle-cell carrier is heterozygous, \(\text{Hb}^{\text{A}}\text{Hb}^{\text{S}}\).

Parents: \(\text{Hb}^{\text{A}}\text{Hb}^{\text{S}} \times \text{Hb}^{\text{A}}\text{Hb}^{\text{S}}\)

Gametes: \(\text{Hb}^{\text{A}}\), \(\text{Hb}^{\text{S}}\) from each parent.

| Gametes | \(\text{Hb}^{\text{A}}\) | \(\text{Hb}^{\text{S}}\) |
|---|---|---|
| \(\text{Hb}^{\text{A}}\) | \(\text{Hb}^{\text{A}}\text{Hb}^{\text{A}}\) (unaffected) | \(\text{Hb}^{\text{A}}\text{Hb}^{\text{S}}\) (carrier) |
| \(\text{Hb}^{\text{S}}\) | \(\text{Hb}^{\text{A}}\text{Hb}^{\text{S}}\) (carrier) | \(\text{Hb}^{\text{S}}\text{Hb}^{\text{S}}\) (affected) |

Ratio of carrier : disease free : diseased = **2 : 1 : 1**.

The substituted base: the disease arises from a single base substitution at the sixth codon of the \(\beta\)-globin gene, GAG changing to GUG in the mRNA. So **adenine is replaced**, by thymine in the gene (by uracil in the mRNA), and as a result glutamic acid is replaced by valine at the sixth position of the \(\beta\)-globin chain of haemoglobin. (The substitution is in the gene; the haemoglobin molecule itself carries the changed amino acid.)

(ii) **Garden pea** shows complete dominance (the Law of Dominance): violet flower colour is dominant over white.

P: WW (violet) \(\times\) ww (white)
Gametes: W and w
\(\text{F}_1\): all Ww, **violet**

Selfing the \(\text{F}_1\) gives an \(\text{F}_2\) of 3 violet : 1 white (genotypes 1 WW : 2 Ww : 1 ww).

**Snapdragon** shows **incomplete dominance**: red is not completely dominant over white, so the heterozygote is intermediate.

P: RR (red) \(\times\) rr (white)
Gametes: R and r
\(\text{F}_1\): all Rr, **pink**

Selfing the \(\text{F}_1\) gives an \(\text{F}_2\) of 1 red (RR) : 2 pink (Rr) : 1 white (rr), so here the phenotypic ratio is the same as the genotypic ratio.

So the difference is that the pea heterozygote looks like the dominant parent, while the snapdragon heterozygote is a new, intermediate (pink) phenotype.

rows.stem:
Explain with the help of well-labelled diagrams how lac operon operates in E. coli :
(i) In presence of an inducer.
(ii) In absence of an inducer.
rows.solution:
The lac operon consists of a regulatory gene (i), a promoter (p), an operator (o) and three structural genes, z, y and a, which code for \(\beta\)-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase. The i gene codes for the repressor of the operon; it is constitutive and makes its repressor mRNA and repressor protein all the time. Lactose is the inducer.

(i) **In presence of an inducer**
The diagram shows the gene row p, i, p, o, z, y, a; repressor mRNA and repressor protein made from i; lactose (the inducer) binding to the repressor; and lac mRNA transcribed from z, y and a, translated into \(\beta\)-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase.
- The inducer (lactose, or allolactose) binds to the repressor and **inactivates** it, so the repressor cannot bind to the operator.
- RNA polymerase can now bind to the promoter and **transcribe the operon** into lac mRNA.
- The lac mRNA is translated into \(\beta\)-galactosidase (which hydrolyses lactose into galactose and glucose), permease (which increases the permeability of the cell to lactose) and transacetylase.

(ii) **In absence of an inducer**
The diagram shows the same gene row, with repressor mRNA and repressor made from i, and the repressor bound to the operator (o).
- The repressor protein **binds to the operator region** of the operon.
- This prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon, so the structural genes are **switched off** and the enzymes are not made.

So the lac operon is under negative regulation: it is switched on only when lactose is present for the cell to use.
